entries.title: Israel releases first of 5 Lebanese prisoners
entries.summary: Israel has agreed to release five civilians in exchange for Lebanese assistance in locating the bodies of missing Lebanese Jewish leaders killed in the 1980s. Talks aimed at ending the war with Hezbollah remain stalled.
entries.content:
Israel

Israel releases first of 5 Lebanese prisoners

September 3, 2026

Israel has agreed to release five civilians in exchange for Lebanese assistance in locating the bodies of missing Lebanese Jewish leaders killed in the 1980s. Talks aimed at ending the war with Hezbollah remain stalled.

A Lebanese man who had been held prisoner in Israel was released on Thursday, the first such handover since the outbreak of the latest conflict between Israel and Hezbollah six months ago.

The release of prisoner Malek Ghazi was confirmed by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which facilitated his handover to the Lebanese army in the city of Tyre, Lebanon.

Ghazi is to be first of five Lebanese civilians detained by Israeli forces in southern Lebanon who Israel has agreed to release.

"After their interrogation was completed, it became clear that they are civilians who are not members of any terrorist organization, have not engaged in terrorism, and there is no reason to continue holding them in Israel," read a statement from the office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Lebanese officials told the AFP news agency that the four remaining prisoners are expected to be released on Friday.

Lebanon thanks US for prisoner release efforts

"We will continue working until all our prisoners are released, the fate of the missing is revealed, and a complete Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory is achieved," read a statement from Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, who also thanked the United States for its "efforts exerted in this regard."

In Washington, the US State Department said the releases were the "result of US-led mediation between two legitimate governments" and were finalized during a recent trip to Israel by the US ambassador to Lebanon, Michel Issa.

"We commend the government of Israel and the government of Lebanon for demonstrating good faith through these initial steps, and hope this will serve as the basis for expanded discussions on other civilian issues," added the statement.

Dozens of Lebanese prisoners are believed to be held in Israeli detention centers, including several Hezbollah militants but also a number of civilians and at least one Syrian national, according to a list of more than 30 people compiled by the prisoners' families.

Why did Israel agree to release Lebanese prisoners?

As part of the deal to secure the release of the detained Lebanese civilians, Lebanon has been assisting in the search for the bodies of Lebanese Jewish leaders who Israel says were "abducted and murdered by terrorist organizations" during the Lebanese civil war in the 1980s.

A Lebanese official told the Associated Press that Lebanese authorities were "actively searching for the bodies of the Lebanese Jewish leaders."

The statement from Netanyahu's office described these "field operations" as "significant activity."

Nevertheless, despite the prisoner release, peace talks remain at an impasse.

In June, Lebanon and Israel signed a US-mediated framework deal under which Israeli forces were to withdraw from southern Lebanon in exchange for the disarmament of Hezbollah. But little progress has been made.

Israel-Lebanon talks remain stalled

The news came as Israeli forces reportedly detained more Lebanese citizens.

Lebanese state media reported that troops had entered the town of Halta in southern Lebanon earlier Thursday and seized three men "after the force surrounded several houses and prevented residents from leaving."

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) did not immediately comment.

"However difficult the negotiation process may seem, we will continue to mobilize all necessary efforts to safeguard Lebanon's rights and the interests of the Lebanese people," said Lebanese Prime Minister Salam ahead of further talks in Rome, Italy, later in September. "Particularly our people in the south."

Hezbollah is not a party to the talks and insists it will not give up its weapons in any area north of southern Lebanon's Litani river.

Israeli officials, meanwhile, have said their forces will not withdraw unless the Iran-backed militia is disarmed throughout Lebanon.

Edited by; Zac Crellin

entries.title: Indonesia: Thousands fall sick from free school meals
entries.summary: Hundreds of new food poisoning cases have been reported this week linked to President Prabowo Subianto's free school lunch program. The costly scheme has been dogged by health concerns and allegations of corruption.
entries.content:
September 3, 2026

Hundreds of new food poisoning cases have been reported this week linked to President Prabowo Subianto's free school lunch program. The costly scheme has been dogged by health concerns and allegations of corruption.

More 1,700 people have contracted food poisoning in Indonesia over the past week after eating free school meals provided by the government as part of a new scheme.

At least 725 pupils and 25 teachers at a school in Lasem on the island of Java complained that they felt unwell on Thursday morning after consuming the free lunch on Wednesday.

"They had diarrhea, they were vomiting, and felt nauseous," said the school's principal. "There was a queue at the bathrooms because two of our toilets are under renovation."

Earlier this week, more than 600 students in Sidoarjo, East Java, were also taken to hospital after eating free lunch meals on Tuesday.

In two other cases on Wednesday, 49 people in the East Java city of Nganjuk and 237 in the West Sumatra region of Agam also fell ill.

One lawmaker, Charles Honoris, put the total number of food poisoning cases linked to the free school meals scheme as high as 50,000 since, citing health department data.

"This is a failure of the ⁠system," he said.

What has caused the food poisoning?

The mass outbreaks of food poisoning have been blamed on improper food storage and late delivery of pre-cooked meals.

According to the school principal in Lasem, a food taster found that some of the grilled chicken to be distributed was "slimy" and therefore put aside.

"The kitchen operator said the food was cooked at 3 a.m. and it ​was eaten at noon," she reported.

President Prabowo's free school meals scheme

The $12.94 -billion (€11.13-billion) program, launched in January 2025, is one of President Prabowo Subianto's signature policies, intended to improve nutrition for up to 80 million children as well as pregnant and breastfeeding women.

But the costly scheme has been dogged by allegations of corruption, ​leadership changes and spate of mass food poisoning outbreaks.

It was among the first budget items to be cut back as the Indonesian government moved to counter the economic impact of the war in the Middle East and hundreds of people took to the streets of the capital, Jakarta, last week to call for it to be scrapped entirely.

"This has become a national alarm," said Ubaid Matraji, a researcher at the Indonesian Education Monitoring Network.

"The government cannot continue to treat them as mere statistical figures. Behind every number there is a sick child, a panicked family, and the state's failure to guarantee safe food."

The head of Indonesia's National Nutrition Agency, ⁠which oversees the scheme, told a parliamentary hearing that the food poisoning cases would be ​handled "seriously."

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Trump's Iran strategy: Could this become a forever war?
entries.summary: The US has launched fresh attacks on military targets in Iran. It wants to prevent Tehran rebuilding its destroyed capabilities, but risks triggering a sustained downward spiral of reconstruction followed by new attacks.
entries.content:
Iran

Trump's Iran strategy: Could this become a forever war?

September 3, 2026

The US has launched fresh attacks on military targets in Iran. It wants to prevent Tehran rebuilding its destroyed capabilities, but risks triggering a sustained downward spiral of reconstruction followed by new attacks.

US President Donald Trump has given a fairly clear description of what the next phase of the Iran war could look like. The Iranians had tried to rebuild their radar equipment, Trump stated after the most recent wave of US strikes. "We waited until it was almost built, and then we hit it," he said.

On Tuesday, American forces once again attacked several targets in Iran. According to US Central Command (CENTCOM), the targets destroyed included "air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites."

'Mowing the grass'

Iran responded by firing rockets and drones at US facilities in the region. With this, the war moved on to what CENTCOM had indicated just a few days earlier could be the strategy for the next phase.

According to the news portal Axios, it was considering limited strikes, at regular intervals if necessary, to prevent Iran from reconstituting its military capabilities in the Strait of Hormuz. An American government representative used a concept from Israeli security policy to describe this idea: He called it "mowing the grass."

The metaphor refers to a strategy that doesn't even attempt to promise that an opponent will be defeated once and for all. It is enough to regularly reduce the enemy's military capabilities to the point where the threat remains manageable. When the grass grows back, you "mow" it again.

Applied to the situation in Iran, this would mean the US keeping an eye on which military capabilities the enemy is reconstituting, and attacking once it crosses a certain threshold.

Successes that won't last

In the past few months, the US has scored some military successes. US forces have significantly reduced Iran's military capabilities in the Strait of Hormuz, and have begun clearing Iranian sea mines.

However, these successes will not last. Tehran is repairing or procuring new radar installations, anti-aircraft positions and anti-ship missiles. US bombs could certainly destroy important Iranian positions with targeted strikes. But the knowledge and the industrial basis of Iranian military technology would remain.

Reconstruction can therefore be delayed, but not prevented. The US will repeatedly be confronted with the same choice: whether to accept that Tehran is regaining its capabilities, or to attack again and destroy them.

Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, warned as early as April that this development could lead to an "enduring low-intensity conflict punctuated by more intensive interventions."

Trump's belligerent warnings

The fact that the strategy of "mowing the grass" is reaching its limits is also because it was never designed for a war with a state. Israel developed the strategy to combat non-state actors like Hamas.

However, as Yacoubian pointed out in her article, the Israeli academics who initially coined the term warned that if the opponent had "statist characteristics and/or more powerful capabilities, 'mowing the grass' might become an outdated military strategy." This is clearly the case with the Strait of Hormuz.

The US needs to keep the strait reliably open. Iran, on the other hand, only needs to make people believe that the passage remains dangerous. In this way, even a significantly weakened opponent can impose substantial costs on Washington.

Another problem for the US is that, while Washington can determine the intensity of its own attacks, it has no control over Tehran's response. This week, Trump warned Tehran not to launch a retaliatory strike, threatening that Iran would be "totally wiped out as a country" if it did.

Nonetheless, the regime in Tehran immediately fired missiles against American facilities in the region. Jordan alone reported 13 ballistic missiles in its airspace, 10 of which it was able to intercept.

The nuclear question

But Yacoubian believes that repeated American attacks carry a far greater risk. She warns that they may lead Tehran to conclude that "pursuit of a nuclear weapon" is the only way to achieve "lasting deterrence." This suggests that, by attacking Iran, the US and Israel could actually accelerate the precise development they sought to bring under control.

From Washington's perspective, the alternatives available to Trump don't look much better. If the president accepts Iran rebuilding its military strength around the Strait of Hormuz, he risks renewed attacks on shipping and disruption of one of the world's most important energy routes.

The consequences for the global economy are well known. In spite of the upheaval and repeated negotiations, a political agreement between Washington and Tehran has so far failed because of apparently insurmountable differences.

America's next 'forever war'?

For Trump, "mowing the grass" has domestic appeal, in spite of the uncertainty it brings to foreign policy. The US president would be able to avoid occupation, nation building and deploying large numbers of American ground troops.

At the same time, it allows him to distance himself from the so-called "forever wars" he repeatedly accused his predecessors in the White House of pursuing.

Ultimately, though, this supposed way of avoiding a forever war could become one of its own. Yacoubian describes it as a "Sisyphean attrition strategy without end." As long as Washington is not prepared at some point to accept the rebuilding of Iran's capabilities, each successful attack merely creates the justification for the next one.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Berlin BER airport Terminal 1 evacuated after security scare
entries.summary: Authorities have emptied Terminal 1 at BER airport in Berlin, at least as a precaution. The airport said that more than two-dozen flights had been delayed but that they were trying to avoid any cancellations.
entries.content:
Germany

Berlin BER airport Terminal 1 evacuated after security scare

September 3, 2026

Authorities have emptied Terminal 1 at BER airport in Berlin, at least as a precaution. The airport said that more than two-dozen flights had been delayed but that they were trying to avoid any cancellations.

Germany's federal police, responsible for transportation security, evacuated Terminal 1 of Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) on Thursday evening. 

Preliminary reports suggested a luggage security scare. It was not immediately clear whether or not it posed a real threat.

A police spokesperson said that a woman had told security staff at a service point that she had a dangerous substance.

"A potential threat from the unidentified substance could not be ruled out," the spokesperson told Germany's DPA news agency.

A hazardous item alert was then issued. The spokesperson declined to comment further at the early stage.

What did the airport say about departures and arrivals?

The airport itself also confirmed the incident slightly later on Thursday.

"Because of the suspicion of a dangerous substance, the federal police issued a dangerous item alert at around 5:45 p.m.," an airport spokesperson said, leading to the "public area of Terminal 1 being cleared."

They said planes that were already prepared to depart could take off as normal and incoming arrivals could also continue to land.

Passenger processing was being "relocated to Terminal 2 to the extent that it's possible," the spokesperson said.

"The degree to which this could lead to delays or cancellations is not yet foreseeable."

Many but not all flights departing Terminal 1 from around 7 p.m. local time were marked as delayed on the airport's website. An airport press officer told DW that around 30 flights had been delayed but that they were trying to avoid cancellations by redirecting departures to Terminal 2.

Trains were also impacted by the operation for a time. The city's S-Bahn train service confirmed disruptions on both lines to airport, while Deutsche Bahn also reported widespread disruptions to regional trains.

BER or the "Willy Brandt Airport" in Schönefeld is Berlin's busiest and Germany's third-busiest airport since it opened in 2020. It also serves as the primary airport for many federal government flights. Some 26 million passengers travel through it each year. 

The last comparable security disruption at the airport was in March of this year, when flights were disrupted but because of a potentially suspicious aerial object rather than a suspicious item in the terminal.

entries.title: Norway seizes Russian ship in Svalbard to compensate Ukraine
entries.summary: Authorities in Norway have seized a Russian ship, the Professor Molchanov, on a court order sought and obtained by Naftogaz in Ukraine. Russia has protested the move, which stems from its refusal to pay Naftogaz damages.
entries.content:
Norway

Norway seizes Russian ship in Svalbard to compensate Ukraine

September 3, 2026

Authorities in Norway have seized a Russian ship, the Professor Molchanov, on a court order sought and obtained by Naftogaz in Ukraine. Russia has protested the move, which stems from its refusal to pay Naftogaz damages.

Norwegian courts have ordered the seizure of a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce part of a $4.22 billion (roughly €3.6 billion) compensation claim won by Ukrainian state energy firm Naftogaz after Moscow's seizure of its assets in Crimea, which Russia illegally annexed in 2014. 

Officials announced that the ship had been stopped from departing the port in the Russian coal mining settlement of Barentsburg in the Svalbard archipelago late on Wednesday.

Svalbard has been Norwegian territory since 1925 but is a demilitarized zone where people from dozens of countries, Russia included, can settle without visas under certain conditions.

Russia's ambassador to Norway said that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels.

What do we know about the Professor Molchanov ship being impounded?

The first group to announce the ship's seizure was Covington, the US law firm representing Naftogaz as it tries to secure the compensation awarded to it by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague in 2023.

Russia had refused to pay the fine plus legal fees and interest amid its ongoing war with Ukraine, and Naftogaz has since begun trying to secure the seizure and forced sale of Russian commercial assets via local courts instead. 

"Russia cannot evade ​responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," said Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko.

Covington said it had been tracking the ship, the Professor Molchanov, for months. It said its application was approved on Monday by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court, which ordered Svalbard's governor to ensure the ship stayed in dock once it arrived.

The Svalbard governor's office later issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held in Svalbard.

"The governor will take care of the crew and passengers on board the vessel in collaboration with Trust Arktikugol," it said, referring to the Russian enterprise (meaning "Arctic Coal") that administers the Barentsburg mining settlement.

Norway's Justice Ministry, meanwhile, said the issue did not directly concern the government in Oslo.

"Russia can demand that ​the district court reassess the case," the Justice ‌Ministry said.

How did Russia respond?

Russia's ambassador to Norway, Nikolai Korchunov, said in a statement on Thursday that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels.

"We insist on the immediate release of the vessel and on ensuring the safety of its passengers and crew," he said.

The Kremlin also summoned Norway's ambassador in Moscow to lodge a formal complaint.

The Professor Molchanov, a repurposed research vessel, arrived in Barentsburg on Tuesday with a party of Russian scientists, according to a journalist who was accompanying them.

"The seizure has had no impact on the expedition participants or the ship's crew. No one has been arrested. We are all going about our business as usual," Andrei Gorbunov, editor-in-chief of Komsomolskaya Pravda (KP) radio wrote on KP's website.

He said that for the time being, "the Professor Molchanov is simply forbidden from leaving the port of Barentsburg," adding it was unclear how long this would remain the case.

What is behind Svalbard's special status, and why is it home to the Barentsburg settlement?

Svalbard is an archipelago well to the north of mainland Norway in the Arctic Circle, sparsely populated and thought to be home to slightly fewer than 3,000 people.

It was a whaling base in the 17th and 18th centuries and became a coal mining site at the beginning of the 20th century.

The territory was recognized as part of Norway in 1925, but only after the 1920 establishment of an international treaty — which nowadays has dozens of signatories — designating the area a demilitarized zone where anybody from a signatory state was permitted to settle and work without a visa, provided they met certain conditions. 

The Soviet Union eventually acquired three sites and developed them as company towns: Barentsburg, with a remnant population of around 300 mostly Russian nationals, the nearly-abandoned settlement of Pyramiden, and Grumant, which has been left as a ghost town for decades.

Tourism has become a growth industry on the stark but stunning polar archipelago.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Germany: From emigration to immigration destination
entries.summary: Migration is a sensitive topic in Germany, with public debate dominated by the fear of uncontrolled immigration. People forget that, over two centuries, millions of Germans emigrated in search of a better life.
entries.content:
September 3, 2026

Migration is a sensitive topic in Germany, with public debate dominated by the fear of uncontrolled immigration. People forget that, over two centuries, millions of Germans emigrated in search of a better life.

"Why should [they] be suffered to swarm into our Settlements, and by herding together establish their Language and Manners to the Exclusion of ours? [...] [They] will shortly be so numerous [...] and will never adopt our Language or Customs."

These defamatory comments about refugees and asylum-seekers sound as if they might have been made today by the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany party (AfD). Yet in this instance, the people vilified and accused of refusing to integrate are Germans — and the harsh judgement was made in the 18th century by none other than Benjamin Franklin, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States.

The pursuit of happiness and a better life are mentioned in the American Declaration of Independence, which Franklin helped write. Over the centuries, they have been the motivation for countless people to turn their backs on their respective homelands.

The Germans who emigrated to America in Franklin's lifetime were actually fairly limited in number. By 1820, only about 150,000 had successfully made the journey. Often, they were persuaded by compatriots who told tales of their tremendous success in their new homeland and celebrated the prosperity they had supposedly attained in a very short space of time. What most people back home didn't know was that these recruiters received a commission for every migrant.

"The crossing on a sailing ship cost about what a tradesman would earn in a year," said Simone Blaschka of the German Emigration Center in Bremerhaven. "To be able to afford that, families had to sell all their worldly goods."

A journey into the unknown

They would have had no idea what awaited them on board the ship. During the crossing, which took several weeks, they were packed together below deck in a very confined space, plagued by bedbugs, fleas and rats. Many fell sick with dysentery, typhoid, smallpox or scurvy.

In his book "Journey to Pennsylvania in the Year 1750," the schoolmaster and organist Gottlieb Mittelberger described what he had experienced on the voyage: "Many people whimper, sigh and cry piteously for their homes; most of them get home-sick. Many hundred people necessarily die and perish in such misery, and must be cast into the sea."

On arrival in America, Mittelberger wrote, the majority of his fellow passengers were effectively auctioned off. These were people without means who were granted free passage after undertaking to work for years as bonded laborers in exchange. In the US, their contracts were sold off. Mittelberger saw families torn apart and parents forced to sell their children.

An invitation from Russia

As these early migrants were traveling to America, there was simultaneously a big wave of emigration from Germany to the east. People followed the call of the Russian czarina, Catherine the Great, herself a German princess by birth.

On July 22, 1763, she issued a manifesto inviting people to come to Russia, with the aim of cultivating uninhabited regions for arable farming. She promised the new arrivals free transport to their chosen place of residence, land, also free of charge, the first year tax-free, schooling, exemption from military service, and a special political status that would allow them to maintain the German language and, for the most part, govern themselves.

However, in the 19th century the American continent once again became the dream destination. "The German population almost doubled in the 19th century, so you can imagine what the job market was like," said Blaschka from the German Emigration Center. The situation was exacerbated by failed harvests and famines.

"People didn't see any future for themselves or their children, and decided to emigrate," she said. In this way, around 6 million Germans were drawn to the New World.

Migration: A burden or an asset?

Germans were far from the only ones who left their homeland.

"Between the beginning of the 19th century and the World War I, there were probably around 60 million Europeans who left their homes," said Jochen Oltmer, a professor at the Institute for Migration Research and Intercultural Studies in Osnabrück. Then, in the mid-20th century, this trend reversed and Europe went from being a continent of emigration to one of immigration.

In the 1950s and '60s, the future looked rosy for postwar West Germany and its "economic miracle." From 1956 onward, so-called "guest worker trains" arrived in stations like Stuttgart, Dortmund and Cologne, carrying Italians, Greeks, Spaniards, Portuguese, Yugoslavs and Turks, attracted by the promise of well-paid jobs in the new Federal Republic.

By the time the ban on recruiting foreign labor came into force in 1973, around 14 million people had come to West Germany as "guest workers." Around 3 million stayed permanently.

Yet Germany still did not consider itself an immigration country. "For a very long time, we were dealing with the mindset: It doesn't matter why people came to the Federal Republic; they don't belong, because in any case they'll leave the country again and disappear," said Oltmer.

In 2025, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office, more than 30% of Germany's total population had a migrant background. Yet many third- and fourth-generation citizens still don't feel they belong, which has to do with the perspective of the society in which they live.

Who's welcome – and who isn't?

These days, Germany is keen to attract skilled workers, but refugees are only granted asylum if they are politically persecuted in their homeland, or are fleeing war.

As a migration researcher, Oltmer is constantly examining the reasons why some migrants are accepted and others are not. This question was especially relevant in 2015, when refugees came to Germany in very large numbers.

"The attitude was: 'OK, you people from Syria, in light of the Syrian civil war, you are entitled to protection.' But at the same time this society says of people from Afghanistan, 'In your case, we're a bit more sceptical,'" he said.

Yet asylum accounts for barely 10% of immigration to Germany, Oltmer explained. The majority of immigrants are not people fleeing their country. "This means that when it comes to scandalization and the creation of certain negative images, we are seeing a massive distortion of the debate." And the descendants of the German emigrants Benjamin Franklin once reviled as "Palatine boors" have long since perfectly integrated into American society.

In Germany, however, integration is taking much longer. "Many people have no possibility of regularizing their status and obtaining a stable residence permit, even though everyone involved knows they can stay, and will stay," said Oltmer. He believes people urgently need to sit down and clarify how they want German society to look in future.

"It may be a very hard, even hurtful discussion. But it's the only way."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: US sanctions halt TOEFL and GRE tests in Iran, disrupting study plans
entries.summary: Students in Iran can no longer take English-language proficiency exams after the suspension of a US sanctions exemption. Applicants say the move threatens university deadlines and adds costly travel obligations.
entries.content:
September 3, 2026

Students in Iran can no longer take English-language proficiency exams after the suspension of a US sanctions exemption. Applicants say the move threatens university deadlines and adds costly travel obligations.

Iranian students hoping to study abroad are facing a new obstacle after TOEFL and GRE testing was suspended inside the country following changes to US sanctions regulations.

"My entire plan was built around taking this exam," a TOEFL candidate in Tehran told DW.

She said she had spent months preparing applications for a Ph.D. program, contacting professors and gathering documents despite internet disruptions and other challenges.

ETS, the US-based organization that administers both English-language proficiency exams, announced it suspended testing in Iran after the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) froze General License G, which had allowed certain educational services to continue in Iran.

"Following OFAC's suspension of General License G, ETS has paused administration of the TOEFL and GRE tests in Iran effective immediately," the organization said in an official notice.

ETS added that Iranian nationals can still take the exams outside Iran and that it is exploring options to restore testing.

TOEFL is a US-based English-language proficiency test accepted by universities worldwide. The GRE is a standardized test required by some graduate programs, particularly in the United States and Canada.

Since the Iran war began in late February, the US has increasingly expanded sanctions targeting Iranian trade and exports, contributing to broader disruptions throughout the Iranian economy.

No timeline for testing to resume

An Iranian institution that administered TOEFL exams told DW that new registrations had stopped following the latest sanctions changes.

The institution added that the suspension could be temporary, but no date had been given for exams to resume.

That uncertainty is particularly serious for students approaching university and scholarship deadlines who have spent months preparing and paying application-related costs.

The suspension follows earlier problems with IELTS (British equivalent of TOEFL) testing in Iran. An IELTS center in Tehran told DW that sanctions-related difficulties transferring money had become one of the main obstacles to continuing exams.

Some Iranian applicants had already been traveling to countries such as Turkey and Armenia to take IELTS. TOEFL and GRE candidates may now have to do the same.

Rising costs for applicants

Alireza, who is preparing to apply to a university in Italy, said the suspension of TOEFL had disrupted a backup plan he had arranged after IELTS testing became unavailable.

"European universities usually accept IELTS. But because IELTS has been suspended in Iran, after extensive correspondence with the university, they agreed to let [Iranian students] meet the required score through an equivalent TOEFL result," he told DW.

"But now TOEFL has also been suspended in Iran. Traveling to a neighboring country just to take the exam is very expensive, especially given Iran's current economic situation," added Alireza.

Another candidate told DW that taking the exam in Turkey or Armenia would mean paying for travel and at least one night's accommodation on top of the test fee.

For students hoping to secure scholarships or full funding, those additional expenses can be significant.

Students launch petition

Iranian TOEFL and GRE candidates have launched an online petition urging ETS to restore access to the exams.

The petition says thousands of students are losing access to tests required for university admissions, scholarships, graduate programs and other academic opportunities. Many, it says, have spent months preparing, paid exam-related costs and built their application schedules around specific test dates.

"Students should not lose years of preparation or their chance to pursue higher education because access to required examinations has suddenly been removed," the petition states.

Narges, an Iranian applicant affected by the suspension, said she had seen the petition circulating in Telegram groups used by language learners and students applying to foreign universities.

"I doubt it will have any impact," she said. "Still, I'm going to sign the petition."

The organizers are calling on the US Treasury Department's OFAC to provide a specific exemption for standardized academic testing, and on ETS to restore TOEFL and GRE services in Iran as soon as legally possible.

They argue that sanctions aimed at the Iranian government should not restrict educational opportunities for ordinary citizens who have no role in state policy.

When sanctions impact education

Until recently, the General License G had provided a legal channel for certain academic exchanges and educational services despite broader US sanctions on Iran.

For many students, the suspension is the latest in a series of barriers to studying abroad.

Bahar, who is applying for Ph.D. programs, said many Iranian students had already shifted their focus from the United States because obtaining visas had become increasingly difficult.

"American universities were our first choice because they generally offer funding for Ph.D. programs more readily than European universities," she told DW.

Now, she said, applicants are increasingly turning to Europe and Australia, but the testing suspension has created a new hurdle.

"There is effectively no difference between IELTS and TOEFL for us now, because in either case, we have to leave Iran to take an English language test," Bahar said.

For students approaching admissions deadlines, postponement may not simply mean waiting a few months. It can mean missing an entire admissions cycle, losing scholarship opportunities or delaying academic plans by a year or more.

While ETS says it is examining possible ways to restore testing in Iran, there is currently no indication of when that might happen. For many applicants, the immediate choice is limited: wait without knowing when testing will return, or spend considerably more to take the same exam abroad.

Edited by: Ole Tangen Jr

entries.title: Putin denies fresh mobilization campaign in Ukraine war
entries.summary: The Russian president said there was no present need to mobilize more men, describing the reports as Ukrainian "disinformation." Putin was speaking during an economic forum in Russia's east.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Putin denies fresh mobilization campaign in Ukraine war

September 3, 2026

The Russian president said there was no present need to mobilize more men, describing the reports as Ukrainian "disinformation." Putin was speaking during an economic forum in Russia's east.

Russia is not preparing to mobilize more men to fight, President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, describing such speculation as Ukrainian "disinformation."

In 2022 and a few months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin ordered the unpopular "partial mobilization" of reservists amid a string of military set backs.

The decision prompted an exodus of draft-age men from Russia and the Kremlin has since repeatedly denied plans for another mobilization.

"There is no scenario today that would require mobilization," Putin told a plenary session of the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.

"This is a disinformation campaign by the enemy in the run-up to the State Duma elections, aimed at influencing the outcome," he added, referring to Russian parliamentary elections later this month. "As is well known, our people enlist voluntarily and sign a contract."

Putin had already dismissed mobilization speculations earlier this week, calling such reports "utter nonsense" and an "information attack" against Russia.

What did Putin say about peace in Ukraine?

Putin once again claimed there was a chance for peace with Ukraine, but stressed the conflict must be resolved by Moscow and Kyiv.

His statements come amid intensified Russian attacks on the Ukrainian capital. Meanwhile, Kyiv has intensified its attacks deeper within Russia, striking online retailers and other civilian targets.

Putin thanked countries which were making an effort to mediate a resolution to the conflict. He said the US and China, among others, were ready to support a peace settlement.

"Ultimately, however, the problem must be resolved ​by the countries involved in the conflict — Russia and Ukraine. ⁠This ​is the correct ​approach. Yet, we are grateful ​to everyone attempting to ‌ contribute to a settlement. Is there ​a ⁠chance? In my view, yes, there is," Putin said.

Still, he went on to condemn Ukraine, saying warnings about risks to planes in Russian airspace amount to "state terrorism." On Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that his country's drones have made Russian airspace unsafe for planes.

How has Moscow responded to Zelenskyy's airspace warning?

On Thursday, Russia's Transport Ministry said it has provided clarifications to foreign airlines about Russian airports' and airspace safety measures.

"They work very closely with us and ​understand all our rules, standards and how we ​ensure flight safety," Russian news agency Interfax ​quoted ‌Transport Minister Andrei Nikitin as saying.

He added that the clarifications were given in response to requests from foreign carriers.

On Wednesday, Russian aviation watchdog Rosaviatsiya stressed in a statement that the country's "air transport, its ground infrastructure, continue to operate ​normally, receiving and dispatching flights, including those of foreign airlines."

European and US carriers have avoided Russian airspace since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. However, other airlines from China, Turkey and the Gulf states still use it.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Can Hichilema heal Zambia's political divide?
entries.summary: The Zambian president starts a second term after a contested election exposed deep political divisions. His challenge now is to unite the country while addressing concerns over political freedoms.
entries.content:
Zambia

Can Hichilema heal Zambia's political divide?

September 3, 2026

The Zambian president starts a second term after a contested election exposed deep political divisions. His challenge now is to unite the country while addressing concerns over political freedoms.

Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema was sworn in for a second five-year term on Tuesday.

For decades, Zambia has worn its peaceful transfers of power almost like a badge of honor in a region where elections have too often ended in disputed results, violence or leaders refusing to leave. Hichilema's own victory in 2021 appeared to strengthen that reputation.

Five years later, the picture is more complicated.

Hichilema begins his second term after a disputed election, with his main challenger facing treason charges, opposition supporters questioning the credibility of the vote and controversy surrounding the closure of courts during the crucial window for election petitions.

Hichilema has promised reconciliation. But for a president who once sat on the other side of power as an opposition leader and treason suspect himself, the test now is whether those words will be matched by the political space he gives his opponents.

Ngobola Cengelo Muyembe, a political, business and social analyst, told DW that reconciliation must begin by recognizing that a significant part of the electorate backed someone else.

"You have to remember that in every 10 people that voted, four people voted for the other side," Muyembe said, noting that during the president's inaugural address, he spoke about reconciliation and uniting people. "But that message can only resonate if what is on the ground reflects what is being spoken about."

Can Hichilema reunite a divided country?

Raymond, a self-employed Zambian who asked that his full name not be used, told DW that Hichilema should look beyond who supported him at the ballot box and govern across Zambia's political and ethnic divisions.

"The president, congratulations! Don't think about people who voted for you, didn't vote for you. One Zambia, one nation, one city," Raymond said. "Real change in mines and agriculture. The mines want us Zambians to be benefiting. Even your Tonga, your Bemba, you are all Zambians."

Artist Mazuba Nzabuka told DW he also wants Hichilema to govern those who supported him and those who did not, while giving young people a greater voice.

"Going forward, he is going to do the promises left behind. He is a president for all people," said Nzabuka. "Those who did not vote for him, those who voted for him. We are the same people. The five years going forward, our voices can be heard. Look after the youths."

But reconciliation will have to contend with the political fallout from the election.

Zambia returned to multiparty democracy in 1991 and has since witnessed several changes of governing parties through elections. Hichilema himself benefited from that tradition when he defeated incumbent President Edgar Lungu in 2021.

The latest election prompted debate about whether that image remains intact.

Democracy faces a new test

The independence of Zambia's institutions may feature prominently during Hichilema's second term.

Critics said their concerns intensified after courts were closed on the final day available for presidential election petitions. Interruptions during the announcement of election results prompted some opposition supporters to question the process.

Analyst Muyembe said that protecting political speech and allowing opponents to openly challenge the government will be crucial to rebuilding confidence.

"If you really respect the people that voted against you, allow them to speak, engage them in a debate, not where you just have to bring in only the people that agree with you and the ones that are talking to themselves on TV, and encourage this national dialogue," Muyembe said.

"Allow the opposition who lost to complain about it the way they want, and then from there you can chart a way forward. But to stifle debate and fudge facts, this is not really helping our democracy."

The arrest of Hichilema's main challenger, Brian Mundubile, and his running mate on treason charges linked to allegations of plotting an armed uprising has become another point of political controversy.

Authorities maintain the case concerns national security, while opposition supporters have questioned the timing of the arrests.

The situation has drawn attention because Hichilema himself once faced a treason charge while in opposition.

The question of whether the institutions that once wielded enormous power over him can operate independently when dealing with his own political opponents is likely to remain part of the debate surrounding his second term.

From economic stability to household relief

Political freedoms are not the only test. Hichilema enters his second term pointing to progress in stabilizing Zambia's economy, including lower inflation and the restructuring of the country's external debt.

But many Zambians are waiting for those gains to reach their homes.

Mutinta Mushabati, who attended Hichilema's inauguration at Heroes Stadium in the capital, Lusaka, told DW that she was encouraged by what she heard from the president.

"That he is going to increase everything, new allowances for school-going children, social cash transfer, CDF," she said, referring to Zambia's expanded Constituency Development Fund, which allocates public money directly to each of the country's constituencies to finance community-driven local development projects and infrastructure.

"I'm very excited right now. I don't even know what I can say. I'm very happy."

Muyembe told DW that the gap between positive national economic indicators and the experience of ordinary households represents a key challenge for Hichilema's second term.

He compared the economy to a reservoir that may be full while the pipes carrying water to individual homes remain blocked.

"Imagine that you got a giant command reservoir that distributes water to houses in the village," the analyst said.

"When the reservoir is full, you have stabilized your macroeconomic arrangement. But if the pipes that take water to the small little villages, the small little houses in these villages, are clogged and blocked, then you haven't really solved the issue because the people need to have the water in their individual houses."

Making Zambia's minerals work for Zambians

Copper and mining remain central to Zambia's economy and could provide one route for translating economic growth into household gains.

Muyembe told DW that Hichilema's government should focus not simply on attracting billions of dollars in investment, but also on ensuring Zambian businesses participate in the supply chains created by that investment.

"If a mine is going to spend $2 billion or $3 billion [€1.7 billion to €2.6 billion] to expand that mine, that $3 billion has to go to the people, the people that are small businesses."

Greater local participation, Muyembe argued, could help create businesses and employment while allowing Zambia to retain more of the wealth generated from its natural resources.

The challenge is particularly important for young Zambians, whose expectations extend beyond political stability to jobs and opportunities.

Five years to shape a legacy

Despite his criticism of the political environment surrounding the election, Muyembe told DW that Hichilema still has an opportunity to determine how his second presidency will ultimately be remembered.

He pointed to former Zambian President Levy Mwanawasa, whose disputed 2001 election was followed by a presidency that later gained broader respect.

"I think he has a chance, basically, to redeem himself from the dent of these elections because it also happened with Mwanawasa. I think Mwanawasa's elections were also looked at funny, but he redeemed himself in the way he governed the following year."

That leaves Hichilema with two closely connected tests over the next five years.

One is economic: whether improving headline indicators can translate into jobs, stronger local businesses and better living standards.

The other is democratic: whether opposition voices can operate freely, institutions can command public trust and political competition can take place without eroding Zambia's long-standing tradition of peaceful transfers of power.

The crowds celebrating at Heroes Stadium showed the hope that still surrounds Hichilema among his supporters. The disputed election and its aftermath revealed the mistrust that exists among many other Zambians.

How he governs both groups may ultimately determine not only Hichilema's legacy, but the kind of democracy Zambia carries into its next political chapter.

This article has been adapted from an episode of DW's AfricaLink podcast.

entries.title: Nvidia to buy Hugging Face in $12.93 billion deal
entries.summary: The AI chip maker said it would keep Hugging Face an open platform that would not require developers to use Nvidia hardware.
entries.content:
September 3, 2026

The AI chip maker said it would keep Hugging Face an open platform that would not require developers to use Nvidia hardware.

Nvidia will acquire artificial intelligence software platform Hugging Face for $12.93 billion (roughly €11.13 billion), the AI chipmaking giant announced on Thursday.

"Together, we will scale Hugging Face's platform, strengthen its infrastructure and expand access to AI for developers and institutions worldwide," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a post on the company's website.

Hugging Face has over 18 million users who have created over 3 million models in over a million applications, according to Nvidia's statement.

Nvidia commits to keeping Hugging Face open

Hugging Face was founded in 2016 by three French entrepreneurs in New York. The company describes itself as "the AI community building the future."

It touts open models that can be downloaded and modified, in contrast to closed models such as rivals OpenAI or Anthropic.

"Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem. Developers will choose the models they want, the frameworks they want, the clouds and inference service providers they want and the computing platforms they want," Huang wrote when announcing the acquisition. "Nvidia compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face."

Nvidia, best known for its GPUs, specialized chips originally designed to render gaming graphics at high speed, has released over 500 models on Hugging Face and more than 250 open datasets.

More companies and software developers have been turning to open models to keep costs down, as they tend to be cheaper than their closed rivals.

Hugging Face co-founder Clem Delangue said he, his two co-founders and the entire Hugging Face would remain on and join Nvidia as part of the new move.

"The goal really is to join Nvidia, to continue to run (an) independently neutral platform within the Nvidia team," he told CNBC.

Hugging Face internal systems broken into by OpenAI

In July, OpenAI said two of its artificial intelligence models hacked into Hugging Face's data processing systems, despite lack of authorization.

The incident fanned concerns that AI giants were incapable of controlling their own technology.

Similar episodes were also reported by Anthropic and Moonshot AI.

Edited by: Zac Crellin
